title: How to Choose a General Contractor in Utah: 8 Things to Check
meta_title: How to Choose a General Contractor in Utah: 8 Things to Check | American Legacy Contracting
meta_description: Learn what to look for when hiring a general contractor in Utah. From license verification to red flags, here are 8 essential things to check before signing a contract.
excerpt: Hiring the wrong contractor can turn your dream project into a nightmare. Here are 8 things every Utah homeowner should check before signing on the dotted line.
content:
Choosing the Right Contractor Makes All the Difference

I've been in the construction industry for over 14 years, and I've seen what happens when homeowners hire the wrong contractor. Unfinished projects, surprise costs, shoddy work that needs to be redone — it's heartbreaking, and it's almost always preventable.

Whether you're planning a basement finish, a kitchen remodel, or a custom home build, the contractor you choose will determine whether your experience is smooth or stressful. Here are the 8 things I always recommend checking before you hire anyone.

1. Check for a Valid Utah Contractor License

This is non-negotiable. In Utah, general contractors are required to hold a valid license issued by the Utah Division of Occupational and Professional Licensing (DOPL). You can verify any contractor's license status on the DOPL website in about 30 seconds.

A valid license means the contractor has met minimum education, experience, and examination requirements. It also means they're accountable — if something goes wrong, there's a licensing board that can step in.

Pro tip: Ask for their license number upfront. Any legitimate contractor will be happy to provide it. If they hesitate or make excuses, that's your first red flag.

2. Verify Insurance Coverage

There are two types of insurance you need to confirm:

  • General liability insurance — This protects your property if something gets damaged during construction.
  • Workers' compensation insurance — This covers workers if they're injured on your property. Without it, you could be held liable.

Don't just take their word for it. Ask for a certificate of insurance and call the insurance company to verify it's current. Policies can lapse, and you don't want to find out the hard way.

3. Look for Relevant Experience and Education

Not all experience is created equal. A contractor who specializes in commercial buildings may not be the best fit for your kitchen remodel, and vice versa.

Ask about their specific experience with projects like yours. How many similar jobs have they completed? Do they have photos or case studies to share?

Education matters too. I hold degrees in Construction Management, which means I don't just know how to build things — I understand project scheduling, cost estimation, building codes, and quality control at a professional level. That kind of background translates directly into a better-run project for you.

4. Read Reviews and Ask for References

Online reviews on Google and Yelp give you a broad picture, but don't stop there. Ask the contractor for 3-5 references from recent projects, and actually call them.

Questions to ask references:

  • Was the project completed on time and on budget?
  • How did the contractor handle unexpected issues?
  • Would you hire them again?
  • How was their communication throughout the project?

Word of mouth is still the most reliable way to find a good contractor in Utah County. Ask neighbors, friends, and family who they've used and whether they'd recommend them.

5. Get Multiple Estimates (and Why Cheapest Isn't Best)

I always recommend getting at least three estimates for any project. This gives you a realistic range of what the work should cost and helps you spot outliers.

Here's the thing most people don't realize: if one bid is significantly lower than the others, that's usually a warning sign, not a bargain. Low bids often mean the contractor is:

  • Cutting corners on materials or labor
  • Underestimating the scope of work (leading to change orders later)
  • Not carrying proper insurance
  • Desperate for work (which can indicate quality or reliability issues)

The best value is a contractor who gives you a thorough, transparent estimate that accounts for everything the project actually requires.

6. Ask About Their Subcontractors

Most general contractors use subcontractors for specialized work like plumbing, electrical, and HVAC. This is normal and expected — but you should know who's actually doing the work in your home.

Ask your contractor:

  • Which portions of the work will be subcontracted?
  • Are the subcontractors licensed and insured?
  • Have they worked with these subs before?
  • Who will be supervising the subcontractors on-site?

A good general contractor has long-standing relationships with reliable subcontractors and takes responsibility for their work quality.

7. Get Everything in Writing

A handshake deal might feel friendly, but it's a recipe for disputes. Your contract should clearly spell out:

  • Scope of work — Exactly what's included (and what's not)
  • Timeline — Start date, milestones, and expected completion
  • Payment schedule — When payments are due and what triggers them
  • Materials — Specific products, brands, and quality levels
  • Change order process — How changes will be handled and priced
  • Warranty — What's covered and for how long

Never pay the full amount upfront. A typical payment structure is 10-30% down, with remaining payments tied to project milestones. In Utah, contractors are limited by law in how much they can collect before starting work.

8. Trust Your Gut — Communication Matters

This one might sound soft, but it's one of the most important factors. You're going to be working closely with this person for weeks or months. How they communicate during the estimate phase tells you a lot about how the project will go.

Good signs:

  • They return calls and emails promptly
  • They listen to your ideas and concerns
  • They explain things clearly without talking down to you
  • They're honest about timelines and potential challenges

If a contractor is hard to reach, dismissive of your questions, or pressures you to sign quickly — move on. The best contractors are confident enough in their work that they don't need high-pressure tactics.

Red Flags to Watch For

Before I wrap up, here are some warning signs that should send you running:

  1. No physical address or office — Legitimate contractors have an established business presence.
  2. Cash-only requests — This often means they're trying to avoid taxes or accountability.
  3. No written estimate — If they won't put it in writing, they're not serious.
  4. Door-to-door solicitation — Especially after storms. Reputable contractors don't need to knock on doors.
  5. Asking for full payment upfront — This is both a red flag and potentially illegal in Utah.
  6. No references or portfolio — Experienced contractors have a track record they're proud to share.
